title: Targeting and Tracking Personality Functioning in Psychotherapy: A Clinical Case Using the Diagnostic Interview for Personality Pathology Based on ICD-11 (DIPP-11).
abstract: Aspects of personality functioning are central to the World Health Organization's ICD-11 dimensional classification of personality disorder and are operationalized in the Diagnostic Interview for Personality Pathology based on ICD-11 (DIPP-11). The present case report illustrates how the DIPP-11 framework may be used to conceptualize, guide, and track psychotherapy with a young man, "Alex," whose stylistic trait presentation was characterized primarily by Negative Affectivity and Detachment in terms of anxiousness, shame, social withdrawal, and emotional inhibition. The report follows Alex before, during, and after a course of eclectic outpatient psychotherapy in a public mental health setting and demonstrates how the 16 DIPP-11 aspects of personality functioning can serve both as treatment targets and as indicators of therapeutic change. The case particularly shows how impairments in self-esteem regulation, self-direction, perspective-taking, emotional regulation, decision-making, and situational-interpersonal appraisal may gradually improve through a combination of supportive psychotherapy, corrective emotional experiences, and the mobilization of fundamental trust. Treatment progress is illustrated through repeated DIPP-11 ratings, showing change as movement from higher to lower dysfunction scores. The case is discussed as an example of how a focus on personality functioning may offer a more dimensional, individualized, recovery-oriented and less stigmatizing approach to psychotherapy with people presenting with personality problems. Clinical implications are considered for treatment planning, outcome monitoring, and service implementation across WHO member states.
